2	name: windows-repo-tool-setup
3	description: "Windows-specific fixes needed to run Google's repo tool for openVela"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: reference
7	  originSessionId: 837cc89b-802e-45d5-8109-6aa2e1994ab5
8	---
9	
10	Getting Google's `repo` tool (launcher at `C:\Users\VICTUS\bin\repo`) to sync openVela on this Windows 11 machine required three fixes. Reuse these if re-syncing or setting up another repo workspace.
11	
12	**Why:** native Windows breaks `repo` in predictable ways.
13	
14	**How to apply:**
15	1. **GPG self-verify fails** (`gpg: Can't check signature` on repo's own tag) → add `--no-repo-verify` to `repo init`.
16	2. **`.repo/repo.tmp` → `.repo/repo` rename `Access denied`** (Windows Defender holds handles on freshly-cloned files) → wait a few seconds and rename via PowerShell `Move-Item`, or just re-run `repo init`.
17	3. **Symlink privilege missing** (`A required privilege is not held by the client` when creating per-project `.git` symlinks) → **Developer Mode must be ON**. Already enabled on this machine via registry `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\AppModelUnlock\AllowDevelopmentWithoutDevLicense = 1` (set with an elevated UAC prompt 2026-06-26). repo passes `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_ALLOW_UNPRIVILEGED_CREATE`, so Dev Mode is enough — no admin/reboot needed.
18	
19	Full init command used:
20	`repo init -u https://github.com/open-vela/contest2026_043_CircuitForge -b dev-ai-contest-2026 -m contest2026_043_CircuitForge.xml --no-repo-verify`
21	then `repo sync -c -j8`.
22	
23	`repo sync` is resumable — if it dies (e.g. disk full), just re-run it; already-fetched projects are skipped. Related: [[openvela-contest-checkout]].

1	---
2	name: openvela-windows-build-recipe
3	description: "How to build openVela for the QEMU emulator on native Windows (works, with patches)"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: reference
7	  originSessionId: 837cc89b-802e-45d5-8109-6aa2e1994ab5
8	---
9	
10	Native-Windows openVela build **works** via the CMake+Ninja path (proven 2026-06-27: full `goldfish-armeabi-v7a-ap` emulator image built — nuttx ELF + nuttx.bin). Do NOT use `build.sh` on Windows (its `-m` path needs Linux `unionfs-fuse`/`fusermount`). Build lives at `D:\openVela` — see [[openvela-contest-checkout]].
11	
12	**Build flow** (Git Bash):
13	```
14	source /d/openVela/vela-env.sh          # sets toolchain PATH + helpers
15	cd /d/openVela/nuttx
16	cmake -B build -DBOARD_CONFIG=$VELA_BOARD_CONFIG -GNinja   # (or: vela_configure)
17	cmake --build build -j8
18	```
19	Artifacts in `nuttx/build/`: `nuttx` (ELF), `nuttx.bin`, `vela_ap.elf/.bin`, `System.map`.
20	
21	**Run in emulator** (boots to NSH `openvela-ap>`, verified 2026-06-27): the goldfish config uses the bundled Android emulator. `emulator.sh` only sets HOST_OS for Linux/Darwin, so force it on Windows:
22	```
23	cd /d/openVela && export HOST_OS=windows HOST_ARCH=x86_64
24	./emulator.sh nuttx/build -no-window     # drop -no-window for the GUI/LCD
25	```
26	It launches `qemu-system-armel-headless.exe -machine virt -cpu cortex-a15 -kernel nuttx/build/nuttx -serial mon:stdio` and even maps the host webcam (NV12) — useful for VelaPaw's camera. Stop with `Stop-Process` on emulator/qemu-system. Non-fatal boot noise: `coredump ... -2` and one `mount failed: 19` (from trimmed config).
27	
28	**One-time setup that was required** (all done):
29	- `pip install kconfiglib pyelftools cxxfilt` INTO the Python CMake auto-selects (`C:/Users/VICTUS/AppData/Local/Python/pythoncore-3.14-64/python.exe`). Put kconfiglib console scripts dir (`AppData/Roaming/Python/Python314/Scripts`) on PATH — vela-env.sh does this.
30	- Windows symlink privilege (Developer Mode) — see [[windows-repo-tool-setup]].
31	
32	**Source patches applied to fix cmd.exe-vs-bash codegen** (3 files in nuttx/):
33	- `cmake/nuttx_multiple_link.cmake`: prefix `mkallsyms.py` with `${Python3_EXECUTABLE}`.
34	- `cmake/nuttx_add_romfs.cmake`: romfs_etc `if [ ]` → plain copy + pipe genromfs/xxd/sed via `bash -c`.
35	- `CMakeLists.txt` (~line 865): System.map `nm|grep|sort` wrapped in `bash -c`.
36	
37	**Config deltas from the stock goldfish defconfig** (disabled to avoid missing optional deps / no host compiler on this machine):
38	- `LV_USE_FREETYPE` off (ft2build.h not on apps include path)
39	- `LV_USE_LIBPNG` off (png.h source not populated; lodepng remains)
40	- `INTERPRETERS_QUICKJS` off (qjsc needs a native host compiler — none installed)
41	- `ALLSYMS` off (post-link uses cxxfilt which can't load libc on Windows)
42	- `FS_NAMED_SEMAPHORES` ON (alsa-lib needs sem_open/sem_close)
43	
44	**Config-change gotcha:** `kconfig-tweak --file build/.config -e/-d SYM` does NOT fill dependent defaults. After tweaking, run `vela_olddefconfig` then re-run `cmake -B build ...` (regenerates config.h). Never delete config.h manually — it's a configure-step output, not a build rule.
45	
46	**Latent limit:** no native host compiler (gcc/clang/cl/mingw) — components that build host tools will fail; install MinGW-w64 if needed. VelaPaw's core (LVGL, camera, tflite-micro) is all cross-compiled, so fine.
47	
48	**Broken apps symlinks (bit us scaffolding an app in packages/demos, 2026-06-27):** `repo` failed to create the 5 `apps/{external,frameworks,packages,tests,vendor}` symlinks on Windows — it left them as **plain text files** containing the relative target (e.g. `../packages`). Each is `add_subdirectory`'d only `if(EXISTS apps/<x>/CMakeLists.txt)`, so as text files they're silently skipped. This meant `packages/demos` (where contest `<linkfile>` apps live) was NEVER buildable. Fix the one(s) you need with a native dir symlink: `cd /d/openVela/apps && MSYS=winsymlinks:nativestrict ln -s ../packages packages`. **Only fix what you need** — fixing `frameworks` pulls in apps with missing generated headers (`topics/algo_amd.h`), and `external/tests/vendor` add more; leave those as text files. After fixing, the stale generated Kconfig aggregator may not refresh — `rm build/apps/Kconfig` then `cmake -B build ...` to force regen of the apps->packages->demos->app Kconfig chain. A new app dir + manifest `<linkfile>` also needs its build-tree symlink created the same way (`ln -s ../../contest2026_043_CircuitForge/app/<x> packages/demos/contest2026_043_<x>`); PowerShell New-Item symlink needs admin, Git Bash ln does not (Developer Mode). The post-generate `ninja -t restat` can blip with `0xc0000142` under load — transient, runs fine standalone; and `-j8` can spuriously kill a compile (no diagnostic) — drop to `-j4` if that happens.
49

9	
10	The mandatory contest AI-Coding log collection is **installed** (2026-06-27) via `contest-log-collector` onboarding. Identity in `~/.claude/contest-collector.env`: **TEAM_ID=contest2026-043, GITHUB_LOGIN=KingMbewe**. Stop/SessionEnd hooks registered in `~/.claude/settings.json` → auto-write sessions to the team repo `logs/<login>/`. Logs live in `D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\logs\KingMbewe\`. See [[openvela-ai-skills]] and [[velapaw-plan]].
11	
12	**Status:** all 8 prior sessions (incl. Phase 0 + TFLM spike) backfilled and validated (`validate-log.py` → ALL OK, 3631 events).
13	
14	**Critical caveats / how to keep it working:**
15	- **Workspace gate:** auto-collection only fires when Claude Code's cwd has `.repo/` upward. The session anchor `C:\Users\VICTUS\openVela` has **no** `.repo` (only D: does). **Launch Claude Code from `D:\openVela`** so future sessions auto-log; otherwise they won't.
16	- **Logs are never auto-pushed.** The tool only writes files. Commit + push yourself: `cd /d/openVela/contest2026_043_CircuitForge && git add logs/ && git commit -s -m "logs: capture session" && git push`.
17	- **Manual backfill workaround:** `export-session.py --backfill` ignores `--github-login` and doesn't pass GITHUB_LOGIN to the snapshot core → "FATAL: cannot detect GITHUB_LOGIN". Fix: `export GITHUB_LOGIN=KingMbewe` before running it. (The auto hook sources contest-collector.env, so it's unaffected.) Command:
18	  `export GITHUB_LOGIN=KingMbewe; python3 <skills>/contest-log-collector/tools/export-session.py --backfill --dest /d/openVela/contest2026_043_CircuitForge --confirm`
19	- **Windows encoding:** the tools print ✅ emoji; on cp1252 consoles set `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 PYTHONUTF8=1` to avoid UnicodeEncodeError.
20	- Don't delete `~/.claude/projects/` history — it's the backfill source if a session was missed.
21	- **Cross-midnight backfill bug (hit & fixed 2026-06-28):** `snapshot_core` writes to *today's* date dir (`local_date()`) and keeps a watermark in BOTH the dest `logs/<login>/manifest.json` and a **staging** copy (`~/.claude/contest-collector-staging/<login>/`). Backfilling one session on multiple days splits it across date dirs, orphaning the older file and breaking `validate-log.py` (event_count mismatch / orphan). It recurs on each NEW day (a different session gets re-split each run). **Simplest robust fix = full clean rebuild** (transcripts in ~/.claude/projects are the source of truth): `rm -rf logs/<login> ~/.claude/contest-collector-staging/<login>` then re-run `export-session.py --backfill ... --confirm` — recreates all 8 sessions fresh, one file each under today's date, consistent manifest. Then `validate-log.py logs/<login>` → ✅ ALL OK. (Per-session repair also works but the full rebuild avoids whack-a-mole.)

1	---
2	name: velapaw-hardware
3	description: "VelaPaw physical build — board choice, BOM, pinout/servo wiring (hardware only; software is in velapaw-plan)"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: project
7	  originSessionId: 837cc89b-802e-45d5-8109-6aa2e1994ab5
8	---
9	
10	VelaPaw **hardware** notes (physical smart-feeder build). Software/firmware is in [[velapaw-plan]]. All decisions below are hardware-only.
11	
12	## Target board (chosen 2026-07-02)
13	**Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C  [with housing-camera]** — item is the SPI variant, NOT the "B".
14	- **3.5-C = SPI / ST7796 display** (easy NuttX port). The **3.5B / 3.5B-C = QSPI** (harder NuttX driver — avoid).
15	- ESP32-S3R8, **8 MB PSRAM, 16 MB flash**; 3.5" 320×480 IPS, **FT6336 capacitive touch** (I2C).
16	- **OV5640 5 MP camera INCLUDED** (with the "-C / with housing-camera" SKU; bare "3.5" has only the connector).
17	- Onboard bonuses: **PCF85063 RTC**, **microSD (TF) slot**, QMI8658 IMU, ES8311 audio, AXP2101 PMIC + battery, **TCA9554 I2C IO-expander**, 2×16 2.54mm GPIO header.
18	- Supersedes the original **ESP32-S3-EYE** (had OV2640 + only a 1.3" 240×240 LCD → too small for the UI). The 3.5-C's big touch screen fits the real LVGL UI.
19	- Buyer note: must pick the "-C [with housing-camera]" line; user needs to add a **microSD card** (slot only).
20	
21	## Bill of materials (to buy / print)
22	- Board: ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C (camera+case included).
23	- **Servo (dispenser):** continuous-rotation micro servo **FS90R** (gentle, ~5V) driving a 3D-printed auger; or MG996R (more torque, needs its own supply). Single servo = single PWM pin.
24	- **Separate 5 V ≥2 A supply** for the servo + **~1000 µF cap** across it; common ground with the board. Do NOT power the servo from the board's 3.3V/LCD rail.
25	- **microSD card** (for persistent feed history).
26	- Jumper wires, M3 screws / heat-set inserts.
27	- **3D-printed (user has a print coupon):** hopper + lid, auger + tube, chute, bowl (or bowl mount), camera/board mount aiming the camera at the bowl, main enclosure.
28	
29	## Pinout (from the official ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5 schematic)
30	Board is nearly fully pinned. Native GPIO map:
31	- LCD (ST7796 SPI): IO1 MOSI, IO2 MISO, IO3 DC, IO4 (QSPI IO3), IO5 SCLK, IO6 BL
32	- I2C bus (touch/RTC/IMU/audio/AXP shared): **IO7 SCL, IO8 SDA**
33	- SD card (SPI): IO9 MISO, IO10 MOSI, IO11 SCLK  (SD_CS on expander EXIO3)
34	- I2S audio (ES8311): IO12 MCLK, IO13 SCLK, IO14 ASDOUT, IO15 LRCK, IO16 DSDIN
35	- Camera (OV5640 DVP): IO17 VSYNC, IO18 HREF, IO21 D7, IO38 XCLK, IO39 D6, IO40 D5, IO41 PCLK, IO42 D4, IO45 D0, IO46 D3, IO47 D1, IO48 D2
36	- USB-C: IO19 (D-), IO20 (D+)
37	- UART0 console: IO43 TXD, IO44 RXD
38	- Flash + octal PSRAM: IO26–37 region (reserved)
39	- IO0: IMU INT + strapping (avoid)
40	- TCA9554 expander EXIO0–7 (all used): CAM_PWDN, LCD_RST, TP_INT, SD_CS, RTC_INT, AXP_IRQ, SYS_OUT, PA_CTRL. Expander is I2C → cannot do servo PWM.
41	
42	## SERVO WIRING DECISION
43	There is **no idle native GPIO** except the UART pins. Plan:
44	- **Servo signal → GPIO43** (LEDC hardware PWM). (GPIO44 available as a 2nd actuator if ever needed.)
45	- **Free IO43/44 by moving the debug console to USB** — use the ESP32-S3 built-in **USB-Serial/JTAG over the USB-C** (IO19/20) instead of UART0. Keeps full logging.
46	- **Servo power: separate 5 V + common ground** (see BOM). Flash/logs over USB-C.
47	- Do NOT use the TCA9554 expander for the servo (I2C too slow for 50 Hz PWM).
48	
49	## Features this board unlocks (deferred in emulator)
50	- **RTC (PCF85063)** → real **meal-timing** (was skipped for lack of a wall clock).
51	- **microSD** → **persistent feed history / analytics** across reboots (was in-memory only).
52	
53	## Feeder dispensing — grams -> motion (calibration)
54	The app speaks **grams** (portions ~5-50g, daily limits 20-300g; NOT kg). The dispenser does not measure grams; it is CALIBRATED once:
55	- Measure kibble released per unit of motion: run the auger 1 rotation (or motor 1 s), weigh the output on a kitchen scale -> e.g. `grams_per_rotation` ~= 5g (or `grams_per_second` ~= 8g). Store the constant (NVS/SD so it survives reboot).
56	- **Dispense N grams = run actuator for N / grams_per_unit** (e.g. 20g @ 5g/rot = 4 rotations, or 2.5s @ 8g/s).
57	- This is OPEN-LOOP feeding (no sensor): ~±10-20% accurate, standard for consumer feeders. Fine for v1.
58	
59	**Firmware hook:** `velapaw_feeder_dispense(grams)` (currently mock print) becomes on hardware: `runtime = grams / grams_per_second; drive_servo(GPIO43 LEDC PWM, runtime);`. Nothing above it changes (app stays in grams). Planned backend: hal/feeder_servo.c.
60	
61	**Accuracy upgrade (deferred):** add a **load cell + HX711** under the bowl -> CLOSED-LOOP: dispense until measured weight == target (~1g accurate). Same hardware also gives real EATEN-grams / eating-speed (the analytics we deferred). Needs the load cell (not on the board).
62	
63	**Suggested (not yet built):** a UI "Calibrate" mode = dispense a test amount -> user weighs it -> enter value -> stores grams_per_unit.
64

2	name: velapaw-plan
3	description: VelaPaw contest product (multi-pet smart feeder) — scope and verified plan corrections
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: project
7	  originSessionId: 837cc89b-802e-45d5-8109-6aa2e1994ab5
8	---
9	
10	**VelaPaw** = the user's contest entry (codename, renameable). A smart pet feeder that recognizes *which individual pet* is at the bowl via on-device camera + INT8 embedding model (open-set metric learning, cosine match — not N-way softmax), dispenses that pet's portion (servo), logs per-pet history. All on-device. Headline differentiator: a live benchmark panel comparing a "fast" MobileNetV3 vs an "accurate" MobileNetV3+TSFM (the user's thesis attention module). Plan doc: `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` (target board ESP32-S3-EYE; emulator-first). See [[openvela-contest-checkout]] and build via [[openvela-windows-build-recipe]].
11	
12	**Phase 0 verified against the real tree (2026-06-27):**
13	- ESP32-S3-EYE board fully supported (camera ov2640, ST7789 LCD, LEDC/PWM for servo, SPIRAM, LVGL all in board defconfig).
14	- TFLite-Micro is in-tree (`apps/mlearning/tflite-micro`, INT8) — there is NO separate "openvela AI framework"; TFLM *is* the AI path. Frame "deep use of AI" as using `apps/mlearning`.
15	- Emulator camera: use `goldfish_camera.c` (real V4L2 virtual cam in QEMU) instead of a file-mock — exercises the real capture API.
16	- KVDB does NOT exist → use `apps/system/settings` (settings.h). Embeddings are binary blobs; verify settings blob support or store as littlefs files.
17	
18	**Three risks flagged (de-risk early):**
19	1. LX7 latency: no ESP-NN found (only cmsis-nn=ARM, nnlib-hifi4=HiFi DSP). Without LX7-optimized kernels, INT8 MobileNetV3 may blow the <300ms target. **Still the #1 open risk** — see TFLM spike below.
20	2. TSFM module + TFLM: TFLM has a fixed op set; custom attention may not quantize/run. Confirm op support before committing it as the headline; fallback = larger plain MobileNetV3.

## The contest
You're on team **contest2026_043_CircuitForge** (team 043) in the **2026 openVela AI Hardware Developer Contest**. Deadline **Sept 20, 2026**, targeting the **AI hardware product** track. Mandatory AI-coding logs must be exported to `logs/KingMbewe/` and committed.

## The environment
- Full openVela checkout is at **`D:\openVela`** (not C: — C: was too small). The session anchor is `C:\Users\VICTUS\openVela` (holds only `.claude`), and the shell resets there, so I use absolute `/d/openVela/...` paths.
- **Windows-native build works** via CMake+Ninja (never `build.sh` — it needs Linux FUSE). Documented patches, config deltas, and the `apps/packages` symlink fix are all captured.
- **Logging** is installed — but only auto-fires when Claude Code is launched from `D:\openVela` (needs `.repo` upward), and logs are never auto-pushed (I commit + push them).

## The product — VelaPaw
A **multi-pet smart feeder**: on-device camera → INT8 embedding model (open-set cosine matching, not softmax) recognizes *which individual pet* is at the bowl → dispenses that pet's portion via servo → logs per-pet history. Headline thesis differentiator: **A/B benchmark of a "fast" MobileNetV3 vs an "accurate" MobileNetV3+TSFM** (your thesis attention module).

Where it stands:
- Device app at `app/velapaw/`, **runs in the emulator** with real TSFM INT8 model (128px, ~565ms/inference), LVGL touch UI (4 tabs: Enroll / Recognize / My Pets / Trends).
- **TSFM thesis result proven**: at 128px, accurate beats fast (margin +33%) — the spatial-attention benefit needs the bigger feature map; at 96px it's starved.
- Features built: per-pet portions, daily limits (hard-capped), feeding analytics (intake/frequency/appetite/drop-alert), interactive Trends chart, standalone **BCS** (body-condition) model with majority-vote, once-per-visit feeding with identity debounce.
- **Live webcam on emulator works via the adb-forward loopback bridge** (`webcam_adb.py`) — the goldfish camera HAL and guest virtio-net are both dead ends; adb was the breakthrough.

## Hardware
Chosen board: **Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C** (SPI/ST7796, OV5640 camera included, 8MB PSRAM). Servo on **GPIO43** (LEDC PWM, console moved to USB-Serial/JTAG to free the pin), separate 5V supply. Feeder is open-loop grams→motion calibration; RTC + microSD unlock meal-timing and persistent history.

Known open items I'd keep in mind: multi-pet recognition discrimination is weak with breed-trained models (needs individual-pet training on your RTX 4060), and analytics/store are still in-memory (persistence to `/data` is the production follow-up).

Good — that check settles the plan. Here's what I found and how we should actually proceed.

## What's true right now
- **VelaPaw code is local-only** (untracked on the team repo), so the VM can't pull it from GitHub. But it's tiny — `app/velapaw` is **3.8 MB** — so transferring it later is trivial. We'll deal with that when we need it.
- **openVela does ship ESP32-S3 boards**: `esp32s3-devkit`, `esp32s3-eye`, `esp32s3-lcd-ev`, `esp32s3-box`, etc. Your **Waveshare 3.5-C is not one of them** — it'll need a custom board config later (the contest `board/contest_board` slot is where that goes).

## Reframing step 5 (important — read this)
"Build the ESP32-S3 firmware then flash" is not one step. Everything in VelaPaw was built and tested on the **goldfish ARM emulator**. The real board is **Xtensa LX7** with real LCD (ST7796), touch (FT6336), camera (OV5640), and servo — none of which exist in the emulator build. That's a **port**, not a recompile, and it's exactly where our flagged risks live (LX7 INT8 latency, custom board bring-up).

So I'm going to stage it. **Milestone 1 = get a stock `esp32s3-devkit` NSH image building in the VM, flashed over USB, booting to a prompt on the board.** That single milestone proves the toolchain, the flash path, and USB passthrough all work — the three things most likely to fight us. *Then* we port VelaPaw on top of a known-good base. Trying to build full VelaPaw for the board in one shot would fail in a dozen places at once with no way to tell which.

## One constraint to be clear about
I'm running on your **Windows host** — I cannot type into the Ubuntu VM. So this is a loop: **I give you a command block, you paste it in the Ubuntu terminal, you paste the output back, I read it and give the next block.** Slower than me driving directly, but it works. Paste errors verbatim and we sort them.

## Block 1 — environment check + build deps (run in the Ubuntu terminal)

This is fast and safe. It verifies the VM, installs NuttX/openVela build dependencies and the `repo` tool, and sets your git identity.

```bash
# --- sanity: version, resources, internet ---
lsb_release -a; echo "---"; nproc; free -h; df -h /; echo "---"; ping -c2 github.com

# --- openVela / NuttX build dependencies ---
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git build-essential gperf flex bison gettext texinfo \
  libncurses-dev libncursesw5-dev pkg-config gawk automake libtool \
  python3 python3-pip python3-venv kconfig-frontends u-boot-tools \
  genromfs xxd unzip curl wget picocom minicom

# --- repo tool ---
mkdir -p ~/bin
curl -sSL https://storage.googleapis.com/git-repo-downloads/repo > ~/bin/repo
chmod a+x ~/bin/repo
echo 'export PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH' >> ~/.bashrc
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH

# --- git identity (contest account) ---
git config --global user.name  "KingMbewe"
git config --global user.email "kingsleymbewe998@gmail.com"
git config --global color.ui   auto

echo "=== BLOCK 1 DONE ==="
```

is it possible to do this on native windows?

Short answer: **the flashing half, yes and it's actually easier on Windows. The building half, technically possible but not worth it — it's the harder of the two environments, and you'd be walking straight back into the shell-script problems we just escaped.** Let me break it down honestly.

## Why native Windows is a bad place to *build* the ESP32-S3 firmware

Remember the emulator build on Windows worked — but only after a pile of patches (the `cmake/nuttx_*.cmake` bash-vs-cmd.exe fixes, config deltas, the broken `apps/packages` symlink). That was for the *goldfish ARM* target, which is relatively simple.

The **ESP32-S3 target is worse on Windows**, because on top of cross-compiling the ELF it adds:
- **A 2nd-stage bootloader + partition-table build step** that pulls in ESP-IDF's build machinery and a bunch of Unix shell scripts. This is the part that reliably fights native Windows.
- More `esptool`/`imgtool` image-assembly steps wired through shell.

So you'd be re-solving Windows-shell whack-a-mole, but harder than last time. The Linux path for ESP32-S3 is the well-trodden one — that's *why* we spun up the VM. The dependency install you just did (Block 1) is already done; throwing it away to re-fight Windows would be a step backward.

## Why native Windows is a *great* place to flash

Flashing is the opposite story:
- The ESP32-S3's USB shows up as a plain **COM port** on Windows.
- `esptool` runs fine on Windows (`pip install esptool`).
- **No USB passthrough needed** — and USB passthrough into a VMware guest is the single fiddliest part of the VM plan (drivers, device capture, permissions).

## My recommendation: the hybrid

**Build in the Linux VM → flash from native Windows.**

1. VM builds the firmware (`nuttx.bin`, `bootloader.bin`, `partition-table.bin`) — the hard part, on the environment that handles it well.
2. Copy those 3 small binaries out to Windows (VMware shared folder, or just `scp`/a USB stick).
3. Flash from a Windows PowerShell with `esptool.py --port COMx write_flash ...` — plug the board straight into your Windows USB, no passthrough.

This gives you the easy build *and* the easy flash, and skips the one VM feature most likely to waste an afternoon.

So: **keep going with the VM sync (Block 2).** When we get to flashing, we'll pull the binaries over to Windows instead of wrestling USB passthrough. Sound good? If so, kick off the `repo sync` and paste the result when it's done.

That's a clear, fixable failure — and it's my miss. The key line is at the bottom:

```
git-lfs filter-process --skip: 1: git-lfs: not found
```

**openVela stores its prebuilt toolchains (the Xtensa/ARM/tricore compilers) via Git LFS**, and `git-lfs` wasn't in the Block 1 package list. Without it, every LFS-backed project (all those `prebuilts_gcc_*`) fails to check out, and the aborted operations left a couple of broken refs behind (the `reference broken` / `Cannot initialize work tree` lines are downstream fallout, not separate problems).

Fix is straightforward: install git-lfs, register it, then re-run the sync (it's resumable and will self-heal the broken refs).

## Block 2b — install git-lfs and resume the sync

```bash
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH
cd ~/openvela

# the missing piece: Git LFS
sudo apt install -y git-lfs
git lfs install          # registers the LFS smudge/clean filters globally

# resume; --force-sync overwrites the half-initialized work trees that broke mid-fetch
repo sync -c -j4 --force-sync

echo "=== BLOCK 2b DONE (exit $?) ==="
df -h /
```

Notes:
- `git lfs install` should print `Git LFS initialized.` — that confirms the filter is registered so checkouts pull the real binaries instead of the tiny pointer files.
- `--force-sync` tells repo to overwrite the projects that were left in a bad state (`Cannot initialize work tree`). Safe here — nothing in this tree is hand-edited yet.
- Still resumable: if it dies again, just re-run `repo sync -c -j4 --force-sync`.

how to make the ubuntu not to go to sleep

Two layers to handle — the desktop's screen-blank/suspend, and (optionally) making sure a long job survives even if the screen locks. For a long `repo sync`, do the GUI setting; the terminal commands are a backup.

## Easiest — GUI (do this one)

1. Open **Settings** (top-right menu → the gear/settings icon, or Activities → search "Settings").
2. **Power**:
   - Set **"Screen Blank"** → **Never**.
   - If there's an **"Automatic Suspend"** toggle → turn it **Off**.
3. **Privacy → Screen Lock** (or **Settings → Privacy**):
   - Turn **"Automatic Screen Lock"** → **Off** (so it doesn't lock mid-sync).

That covers 99% of it.

## Terminal backup (if the GUI options are missing or you prefer commands)

Run these in the Ubuntu terminal — they disable idle blanking and suspend for GNOME:

```bash
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.session idle-delay 0
gsettings set org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power sleep-inactive-ac-type 'nothing'
gsettings set org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.power sleep-inactive-battery-type 'nothing'
gsettings set org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled false
```

`idle-delay 0` = screen never blanks; the `sleep-inactive-*-type 'nothing'` = never auto-suspend.

## Important note for your case

- **The sync keeps running even if the screen blanks or locks** — blanking/locking doesn't kill the terminal process. So even if you forget this, `repo sync` won't die from the screen turning off. What you're really preventing is the *whole VM suspending*, which the settings above stop.
- **Also check VMware itself**: make sure Windows (the host) isn't set to sleep, and in VMware the VM's power settings aren't suspending it. If the *host* Windows sleeps, the VM pauses with it — so on the Windows side, set **Windows → Settings → Power → Screen and sleep → "When plugged in, put my device to sleep" → Never** while the build runs.

Once that's set, let the `repo sync` (Block 2c) run to completion and paste the output back.

Good — that one fact changes the calculus a lot. Here's the honest picture.

## Direct answer: don't turn the VPN off *while syncing from GitHub*

Right now the sync is pulling from **github.com**, which is blocked/throttled in China. Your VPN is the only reason it works at all. If you turn the VPN off mid-sync:
- The active GitHub connections **die instantly** → the sync fails/hangs.
- It's resumable, but you'd just be resuming into a dead connection, so nothing downloads.

So: **VPN stays ON as long as we're on GitHub.**

Also worth knowing — the VPN is very likely *part of why it's slow*. You're going China → VPN tunnel → GitHub → LFS, with packet loss and tunnel overhead stacked on top of GitHub's throttling. That's the ~2 MB/s you're seeing.

## The better path for China: Gitee (no VPN needed at all)

openVela is a Xiaomi project and mirrors to **Gitee**, which is a *domestic Chinese host*. From your location Gitee is fast and needs **no VPN** — in fact VPN OFF is *better* for Gitee, because you'd route directly instead of bouncing through a foreign exit node.

If we can pull from Gitee, then turning the VPN off is not just safe, it's the right move. **But there's a catch I have to verify first:** the *contest* manifest itself lives on GitHub, and I'm not 100% sure every one of the 248 projects (especially the LFS toolchains) has a clean Gitee mirror at a matching path. I don't want to send you into a broken half-mirror.

## Let's test it (this decides everything)

Since the GitHub sync is only ~10% and fully resumable, losing it costs nothing. Do this:

1. **Stop the current sync**: click the terminal, press **`Ctrl+C`**.
2. **Turn the VPN OFF.**
3. Run this reachability test in the Ubuntu terminal:

```bash

  if ! ${BEAR} make -C ${NUTTXDIR} EXTRAFLAGS="$EXTRA_FLAGS" ${@:2}; then
    echo "Error: ############# build ${1} fail ##############"
    exit 2
  else
    if [ -f "${COMPILE_COMMANDS}" ]; then
      cp ${COMPILE_COMMANDS} ${COMPILE_COMMANDS_BACKUP}
    fi
  fi

  if echo "${@:2}" | grep -q "distclean"; then
    if [ -f "${COMPILE_COMMANDS}" ]; then
      rm -rf ${COMPILE_COMMANDS}
    fi
    return;
  fi

  if ! make -C ${NUTTXDIR} savedefconfig; then
    echo "Error: ############# save ${1} fail ##############"
    exit 3
  fi

  if [ ! -d $1 ]; then
    cp ${NUTTXDIR}/defconfig ${ROOTDIR}/nuttx/boards/*/*/${1/[:|\/]//configs/}
  else
    if grep -q "#include" "$1/defconfig"; then
      echo "Note: skipping savedefconfig for debug defconfig."
    else
      cp ${NUTTXDIR}/defconfig $1
    fi
  fi
}

function build_board_cmake()
{
  # first check if the command target is `distclean`
  # cmake is built for out-of-tree, so delete the CMAKE_BINARY_DIR directory directly
  if echo "${@:2}" | grep -q "distclean"; then
    echo -e "Build target distclean:"
    echo -e "  there is no need to distclean in cmake, delete '${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}' directly"
    if [ -d "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}" ]; then
      rm -rf $CMAKE_BINARY_DIR
    fi
    return 0
  fi
  # check parallelism
  j_arg=$(echo ${@:2} |grep -oP '\-j[0-9]+')
  # cmake verbose
  v_arg=""

  # remove the -Wno-cpp build option from ghs build options
  GHS_OPTS_STRING="CONFIG_ARM_TOOLCHAIN_GHS=y"
  TASKING_OPTS_STRING="CONFIG_TRICORE_TOOLCHAIN_TASKING=y"
  defconfig_path=$1/defconfig
  valid_defconfig_path=$(echo ${defconfig_path} | sed 's/^.\{3\}//')
  if grep -qE "^(${GHS_OPTS_STRING}|${TASKING_OPTS_STRING})$" "${valid_defconfig_path}"; then
    echo "EXTRA_FLAGS are required to update the when using the GHS toolchain."
    EXTRA_FLAGS=$(echo "$EXTRA_FLAGS" | sed 's/-Wno-cpp//' | xargs)
  fi
  export VELA_EXTRA_FLAGS="$EXTRA_FLAGS"
  # let use lunch directily
  echo " lunch $1 ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR} "
  lunch $1 ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}
  echo
  # check if the command target is `Xconfig`
  for arg in "${@:2}"
  do
    if [[ $arg == *config ]]; then
      if ! m $arg; then
        echo "Error: #############  m $arg fail ##############"
        exit 2
      else
        return 0
      fi
    fi
    if [[ "$arg" =~ ^V=1$ ]]; then
      v_arg+="V=1"
    fi
  done
  # do cmake build
  if ! m $j_arg $v_arg; then
    echo "Error: ############# build ${1} fail ##############"
    exit 2
  fi
}

Now it's clear — and simpler than expected. The `unionfs-fuse` mount **only happens with the `-m` (out-of-tree) flag**. A plain **in-tree build needs no FUSE at all**: without `-m`, it just sets `NUTTXDIR=nuttx` and runs `configure.sh` + `make`. And it `source`s `build/envsetup.sh`, which sets up the toolchain environment. So the first build is a one-liner.

## Block 5 — Milestone 1: build `esp32s3-devkit:nsh`

```bash
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH
cd ~/openvela

# in-tree build of the canonical smoke-test config; log everything
./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:nsh -j4 2>&1 | tee ~/build-nsh.log

echo "=== BUILD EXIT ${PIPESTATUS[0]} ==="
ls -lh nuttx/nuttx nuttx/nuttx.bin 2>/dev/null
```

What to expect:
- This compiles the **whole RTOS from scratch** — a few minutes on 4 cores. Lots of scrolling `CC ...` lines is normal.
- **Success looks like**: `=== BUILD EXIT 0 ===` and a `nuttx` ELF + `nuttx.bin` listed at the end.
- **This is a first hardware build, so a missing-tool stumble is likely and fine** — the usual suspects are `esptool` (needed to assemble the ESP32 image) or a Python 3.14 hiccup in a build script. We fix those iteratively; don't worry if it doesn't go green first try.

If it **fails**, grab the actual error lines so I can pinpoint it:

```bash
grep -iE "error|fatal|not found|no such|command not|Traceback" ~/build-nsh.log | head -40
```

without vpn ?

Yes — **run it without VPN.** The build is a local compile: all the source and the toolchain are already on disk from the sync. No download needed to compile.

The one caveat: *if* the ESP32-S3 build tries to fetch something mid-build (e.g. a bootloader blob or the ESP HAL), that git fetch will go through the **Gitee redirect** you set up — so still no VPN. VPN off is correct.

The only thing that could trip it is a build step reaching a server we *didn't* redirect (like Espressif's or PyPI). If that happens you'll see a clear network error in the log, and we'll just flip the VPN on for that one step. But start with **VPN off** — most likely it compiles start to finish with no network at all.

That rules out my theory cleanly — the pin **is** an exact SHA (`ESP_HAL_3RDPARTY_VERSION = 9fc713a95b...`), and the build checked out exactly that commit, so the HAL is the *correct* version, not skewed. This is a genuine type conflict: `lock_type_t` is resolving to a **struct**, so the HAL's `= 0` initializer is illegal. That almost always means a wrong/missing OS-port header is defining `lock_type_t` (e.g., NuttX's `<sys/lock.h>` leaking in instead of the HAL's own definition).

I can't see the cloned HAL source from here (it only exists on the VM), so let me get the actual definitions. This tells us whether it's a missing `CONFIG_` define or a header-include-order bug, which determines the fix.

## Diagnostic — dump the conflicting types (VM, no build, fast)

```bash
cd ~/openvela/nuttx

F=$(find arch/xtensa/src -path '*esp_hw_support/clk_ctrl_os.c' | head -1)
echo "FILE: $F"
echo "=== top of the file: includes + the macro + the failing line ==="
sed -n '1,45p' "$F"

echo ""
echo "=== the #if context around LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED ==="
grep -rn -B6 -A2 "define LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED" "$F"

echo ""
echo "=== where is lock_type_t defined, and to WHAT? ==="
grep -rn "lock_type_t" $(dirname "$F")/../.. 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "typedef|} *lock_type_t|define +lock_type_t" | head
echo "--- does NuttX itself define lock_type_t? ---"
grep -rn "lock_type_t" include/sys/lock.h include/ 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "typedef|}|define" | head
```

Paste all of it. What I'm looking for:
- The **`#include`s at the top** of `clk_ctrl_os.c` — is it pulling a NuttX system header for locks?
- The **`#if`/`#ifdef` guarding `LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED 0`** — there's almost certainly an `#else` branch with a struct initializer, and we're taking the wrong branch because a `CONFIG_` macro isn't defined.
- **What `lock_type_t` actually is** — if NuttX defines it as a `struct`, that's the collision.

Once I see those three things, the fix is usually one of: define the missing config macro, or add a small include-path/`-D` correction in the esp32s3 Make.defs. This is the normal kind of first-board-bring-up snag — we patch it and keep going.

text:
Confirmed the root cause precisely. In this NuttX, `spinlock_t` is **always a struct** — every variant in `spinlock_type.h` ends in `} spinlock_t;`, and the correct initializer is the macro **`SP_UNLOCKED`** (`{}` / `{...0}`), never `0`. So the pinned esp-hal (`9fc713a`) is simply **older than this NuttX's struct-based spinlock** — a version-skew bug on the contest branch (they tested the ARM emulator, not ESP32-S3, so this never got caught). A config toggle can't help because there's no scalar `spinlock_t` variant here; the fix is to make the HAL use `SP_UNLOCKED`.

It's a one-token patch, in the `#ifdef __NuttX__` branch only (the `#else` FreeRTOS branch is untouched).

## Block 6 — patch the HAL spinlock init, rebuild

```bash
cd ~/openvela/nuttx
HAL=arch/xtensa/src/esp32s3/esp-hal-3rdparty

echo "=== files with the bad initializer (NuttX branch: '...UNLOCKED  0') ==="
grep -rlE 'define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+0[[:space:]]*$' "$HAL"

# replace the scalar 0 with NuttX's struct initializer SP_UNLOCKED (NuttX branch only)
grep -rlE 'define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+0[[:space:]]*$' "$HAL" \
  | xargs -r sed -i -E 's/(define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+)0[[:space:]]*$/\1SP_UNLOCKED/'

echo "=== after patch (should show SP_UNLOCKED) ==="
grep -rnE 'define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED' "$HAL"

echo "=== rebuild ==="
cd ~/openvela
./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:nsh -j4 2>&1 | tee ~/build-nsh.log
echo "=== BUILD EXIT ${PIPESTATUS[0]} ==="
ls -lh nuttx/nuttx nuttx/nuttx.bin 2>/dev/null
```

Notes:
- The `grep -rl` before/after shows which files changed (expect `clk_ctrl_os.c`, maybe `modem_clock.c`) and confirms they now say `SP_UNLOCKED`.
- The rebuild is **incremental** — it won't re-clone the HAL (it's stamped), and re-checking-out the same SHA leaves our working-tree edit intact. So the patch survives into the compile.

---
name: openvela-esp32s3-vm-build
description: "How to build openVela ESP32-S3 firmware in a Linux VM (China/Gitee, the patches needed, esptool). Milestone 1 build works."
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Building openVela for the **real ESP32-S3 board** (Waveshare, see [[velapaw-hardware]]) is done in a **Linux VM**, not native Windows — the esp32s3 target adds a 2nd-stage/HAL build + shell scripts that are worse on Windows than the emulator was ([[openvela-windows-build-recipe]] is emulator-only). Setup: **VMware + Ubuntu 26.04** (bleeding-edge: system Python is **3.14**, GCC 15). VM at 4 CPU / 7.2 GB / 89 GB disk. Tree lives at **`~/openvela`** on the VM (login `king`). **Milestone 1 (build stock `esp32s3-devkit:nsh`) SUCCEEDED 2026-07-05** → `nuttx/nuttx.bin` 203 KB.

**The user is in China on a flaky VPN. GitHub/LFS over VPN was ~2 MB/s; Gitee (domestic, no VPN) is ~10×.** Decisive lever. See [[windows-repo-tool-setup]] for the original GitHub sync.

## Repo sync (do this on the VM)
- Deps: `git build-essential gperf flex bison gettext texinfo libncurses-dev pkg-config gawk automake libtool python3 python3-pip python3-venv kconfig-frontends u-boot-tools genromfs xxd`. **CRITICAL: also `git-lfs` then `git lfs install`** — openVela toolchains are LFS; without it the sync corrupts (broken refs, "not a git repository"). If corrupted, `rm -rf ~/openvela` and re-init clean.
- `repo` tool → `~/bin/repo`; init `-u https://github.com/open-vela/contest2026_043_CircuitForge -b dev-ai-contest-2026 -m contest2026_043_CircuitForge.xml --no-repo-verify`.
- **Gitee redirect (no VPN, fast):** manifest uses RELATIVE fetch URLs across TWO orgs — `open-vela` (remote "openvela") and `openvela-toolchain-external` (remote "git", e.g. the xtensa-esp32s3 gcc). Both mirror to Gitee; the per-team contest repo is **GitHub-only (404 on Gitee)**. So set 3 git rules and `repo sync -c -j4` VPN-off:
  ```
  git config --global url."https://gitee.com/open-vela/".insteadOf "https://github.com/open-vela/"
  git config --global url."https://gitee.com/openvela-toolchain-external/".insteadOf "https://github.com/openvela-toolchain-external/"
  git config --global url."https://github.com/open-vela/contest2026_043_CircuitForge".insteadOf "https://github.com/open-vela/contest2026_043_CircuitForge"
  ```
  (3rd rule = longest-match exemption so the contest repo stays on GitHub.) Full tree ≈ 30 GB, minutes on Gitee. Verify LFS worked: `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-gcc --version` must run (→ crosstool-NG esp-12.2.0). Also `pip`: use China mirror `https://pypi.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/simple` (no VPN).

## Build (`cd ~/openvela && ./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:nsh -j4`)
`build.sh` in-tree (no `-m`) needs **no unionfs-fuse** (that's only for `-m` out-of-tree). Three fixes were required, all real:
1. **Toolchain not on PATH** — `envsetup.sh` does NOT add the cross-gcc. Add: `export PATH=$HOME/openvela/prebuilts/gcc/linux-x86_64/xtensa-esp32s3-elf/bin:$PATH` (put in `~/.bashrc`). Symptom without it: `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-gcc: command not found` ×hundreds.
2. **esp-hal spinlock skew (contest-branch bug)** — pinned esp-hal `9fc713a` (`ESP_HAL_3RDPARTY_VERSION` in `nuttx/arch/xtensa/src/esp32s3/Make.defs`) predates NuttX making `spinlock_t` a **struct**. `clk_ctrl_os.c`/`modem_clock.c` do `lock_type_t x = LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED` (=`0`) → "invalid initializer". Fix (patch the cloned HAL, NuttX branch only): sed `#define LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED 0` → `SP_UNLOCKED` (NuttX's struct initializer). Config can't fix it — no scalar spinlock_t variant exists. NOTE: this patches cloned 3rd-party source; survives incremental rebuild but a `distclean`/re-clone reverts it — re-apply.
3. **esptool for the image step** — `nuttx/tools/espressif/check_esptool.py` does `importlib.metadata.version("esptool")` with **system python3**, so pipx isolation is INVISIBLE to it. Must install into system python: `python3 -m pip install --break-system-packages esptool` (5.3.1 installs fine on 3.14, builds cp314 wheels). MIN_VERSION 4.8.0; esptool 5's `elf2image` CLI still works.

## Flashing (next milestone — do from Windows, not VM USB-passthrough)
Config uses **SIMPLE BOOT** (`--ram-only-header`) → flash **one file, `nuttx.bin`, at offset `0x0`** (no bootloader/partition table). Build baked `-fs 4MB -fm dio -ff 40m`. Plan: copy `nuttx.bin` to Windows, `pip install esptool` on Windows, plug board into Windows USB (no VMware passthrough), find COM port, `esptool -c esp32s3 write_flash 0x0 nuttx.bin`. **Open question:** `nsh` console = UART0 (GPIO43/44). If the Waveshare USB-C is the ESP32-S3 **native USB** (likely, per [[velapaw-hardware]] servo plan), we won't SEE nsh over USB-C → may need to rebuild `esp32s3-devkit:usbnsh` (console over USB-Serial/JTAG). Decide by how the board enumerates on Windows. VelaPaw port ([[velapaw-plan]]) comes after board bring-up; Waveshare needs a custom board dir (contest `board/contest_board` slot) based on esp32s3-devkit/esp32s3-lcd-ev.

text:
Saved to memory. Here's where we stand and what's next.

## ✅ Milestone 1 (build) — complete
Real ESP32-S3 openVela firmware builds on your Linux VM. Every blocker is now documented: the Gitee redirect (no VPN), the toolchain PATH, the esp-hal spinlock patch, and esptool-into-system-python. `nuttx.bin` is sitting at `~/openvela/nuttx/nuttx.bin`.

## → Milestone 2: flash it to the board (from Windows)
Because it's **simple boot**, flashing is one command with one file:
```
esptool -c esp32s3 write_flash 0x0 nuttx.bin
```
The plan (the hybrid we agreed on — build in VM, flash from Windows, no USB passthrough):
1. Copy `nuttx.bin` from the VM to Windows (shared folder / scp / even a quick upload).
2. `pip install esptool` on Windows.
3. Plug the board into a **Windows** USB port → it appears as a `COM` port.
4. Flash to `COM<x>` at `0x0`.

One thing I need to resolve at flash time: the `nsh` config puts its console on **UART0 (GPIO43/44)**. If your Waveshare board's USB-C is wired to the ESP32-S3's **native USB** (likely, given the plan to run the servo on GPIO43), we'll be able to *flash* fine but might not *see* the NSH prompt over that USB-C — in which case we rebuild `esp32s3-devkit:usbnsh` (console over USB-Serial/JTAG). How the board enumerates on Windows will tell us which. So that's a quick possible detour, not a problem.

**The gating question:** do you physically have the **Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C board in hand** and a USB-C cable? 

- **If yes** → plug it into your Windows machine and tell me how it shows up (a new `COM` port in Device Manager, and its name — e.g. "USB Serial Device", "USB JTAG/serial debug unit", or a "CP210x/CH34x" bridge). That single detail tells me the console situation, then I'll walk you through installing esptool on Windows and flashing.
- **If not yet** → we can't flash, but the time isn't wasted: I'd instead build the **`usbnsh`** variant now (so it's ready), and/or start the **Waveshare custom board** dir and the VelaPaw port so we're ready the moment the board arrives.

Which is it — board in hand or not yet?
board in hand

Board in hand — let's find it. Since I'm running on your Windows machine, I can detect the port directly rather than have you dig through Device Manager. First let me snapshot what serial ports exist **right now, before you plug it in**, so we can spot the new one.

text:
Good — **baseline is zero COM ports** (nothing plugged in), so whatever appears next *is* your board. Clean.

Now:

1. **Plug the board into a USB-C port on your Windows laptop** (not the VM — directly into Windows). Use a **data** USB-C cable, not a charge-only one — if the board only powers on (LCD backlight/LED) but no COM port shows up, the cable is charge-only; swap it.
2. Give Windows ~10 seconds to enumerate it (it may briefly install a driver the first time — the ESP32-S3 native USB is driverless on Win11; a CP210x/CH34x bridge auto-installs).
3. Reply here once it's plugged in.

Then I'll re-scan and we'll see exactly how it shows up. That name is the key clue:
- **"USB JTAG/serial debug unit" (VID 303A)** → native USB-Serial/JTAG → the `nsh` UART console *won't* appear here, so we'll likely rebuild `usbnsh`. But flashing works great.
- **"CP210x" / "CH340" / "USB-Enhanced-SERIAL" (VID 10C4 / 1A86)** → a UART bridge wired to UART0 → the `nsh` console *will* come out here directly. Best case.
- **Both** (some boards expose two ports) → even better, we can use each for its job.

Plug it in and say the word.
plugged

That screen tells us two useful things: the board is **alive and working** (LCD renders, it booted its factory firmware), and that factory firmware is the **Xiaozhi (小智) AI assistant** demo — it's in WiFi-config mode, broadcasting hotspot `Xiaozhi-7EF9`. We'll overwrite that with our `nuttx.bin`, but it confirms the hardware is healthy. Let me find the COM port now.

No COM port on Windows — only internal Intel motherboard controllers, none of which is the board. Given your VM is running, the most likely explanation is that **VMware grabbed the board's USB and handed it straight to the Ubuntu guest** (VMware auto-connects USB devices to a running VM). That's actually *convenient* — if it's in the VM, we flash **directly from Linux**, where esptool and `nuttx.bin` already live. No file transfer, no Windows setup. That's simpler than the hybrid plan.

Let me confirm where the device went. In the **Ubuntu VM terminal**, run:

```bash
echo "=== serial devices present ==="
ls -l /dev/ttyACM* /dev/ttyUSB* 2>/dev/null || echo "(none)"
echo "=== last USB kernel messages ==="
sudo dmesg | grep -iE "usb|tty|cp210|ch34|acm|espressif|jtag" | tail -20
```

What it tells us:
- **`/dev/ttyACM0` appears** (and dmesg shows `cdc_acm` / `Espressif` / `USB JTAG/serial`) → the board's **native USB-Serial/JTAG** is passed into the VM. We flash from Linux via `/dev/ttyACM0`. (This also means the `nsh` UART console won't show on it — we'd rebuild `usbnsh` — but flashing works.)
- **`/dev/ttyUSB0` appears** (dmesg shows `cp210x` / `ch341`) → a UART bridge is in the VM, wired to UART0 → `nsh` console *will* work over it. Best case.
- **`(none)` and nothing new in dmesg** → the device didn't reach the VM either, which points to a **charge-only USB-C cable** (very common) — swap to a known data cable and re-plug.

Also, in VMware's menu bar, check **VM → Removable Devices** — you should see an entry like *"Espressif USB JTAG/serial"* or a *"CH340/CP2102"*, and whether it's connected to the guest. If it's there, it's in the VM.

Run that and paste the output. Whichever way it went, we're one step from flashing — and if it's in the VM, we can flash right now without touching Windows at all.

So the board reached **neither Windows nor the VM**. It's clearly powered (screen's on), but its **USB data isn't being seen anywhere.**

That signature — powers up, no data enumeration on any OS — is almost always one of these, in order of likelihood:

1. **Charge-only USB-C cable.** The #1 cause. Cheap cables (especially ones bundled with gadgets) carry power but no data lines. → **Swap to a cable you *know* does data** (e.g. one you've used to transfer files from a phone to a PC).
2. **Wrong port on the board.** Some ESP32-S3 boards have **two USB-C ports** — one power-only, one for data. → If yours has two, try the other one.
3. Plugged through a **dock/hub** with a charge-only port → plug **directly** into the laptop.

Do this:

2. In the **Ubuntu terminal**, watch for it live — run this, then plug in:

It doesn't block the flash test — any ESP32-S3 takes our image — but the *exact* board matters later for the custom board config. If it has model markings on the back, a photo would help.
- Whichever OS ends up seeing it is fine: if it lands in the **VM**, we flash from Linux directly (easiest); if **Windows**, we do the hybrid. Let's just get it enumerating first.

Windows still sees **nothing** — no COM port, no Espressif/CP210x/CH34x/FTDI device at all. I've now checked twice; the board's USB data is definitively not reaching Windows.

So the answer is on the **VM side + the physical layer**. I need the one thing I don't have yet: **what `dmesg -w` showed when you plugged in.** Let's make it a clean, decisive test — this will tell us in 5 seconds whether it's a dead cable/port or something fixable in software.

In the **Ubuntu terminal**:

```bash
sudo dmesg -C        # clear the log so it's easy to read
sudo dmesg -w        # now watch live
```

Then, while `dmesg -w` is running and watching:
1. **Unplug** the board, wait 2 seconds, **plug it back in.**
2. Watch the terminal for **any** new lines.

Interpretation:
- **Zero new lines** on unplug/replug → the data path is dead. It's a **charge-only cable** or a **power-only port**. Confirm you actually swapped to a *data* cable (the earlier screen-on-but-no-data is the classic charge-cable symptom). No software can fix this — it's the cable/port.
- **Lines appear** mentioning `usb ... idVendor=303a` / `cdc_acm` / `ttyACM0`, or `cp210x` / `ch341` / `ttyUSB0` → it's alive; we're in business and I'll give you the flash command immediately.
- **Lines appear but it errors** (e.g. `device descriptor read error`, `unable to enumerate`) → marginal cable/power; try a shorter/better cable or a different port.

Press `Ctrl+C` to stop the watch, then paste whatever appeared (even "nothing").

Two quick confirmations while you're at it:
- **Did you swap to a known-data cable?** (yes/no — this is the single most likely fix)
- **Does the board have more than one USB-C port**, or just the one you're using?

And if it has a **BOOT button**, try this variant: with `dmesg -w` watching, **hold BOOT, tap RESET/EN, release BOOT** — that forces the ESP32-S3 ROM into download mode, which enumerates its USB even if the running firmware wasn't. If it shows up *then*, flashing will work fine.
take a look

That photo is genuinely useful — it says **`esp32-s3-touch-lcd-3.5 / 2.2.6`**. So this **is** the planned Waveshare **ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5** board (running Xiaozhi firmware v2.2.6). Good — the board is confirmed correct, and per its schematic the **USB-C is wired to the ESP32-S3's native USB** (IO19/20). That means with a *data* cable it should enumerate as a "USB JTAG/serial debug unit."

But I still can't tell you the flash command until we get it to enumerate, and photos of the screen can't tell me that — **I need the terminal output.** The board powering on (screen, reboot on replug) only proves power is flowing; it says nothing about the data lines. Powers-on-but-no-data-anywhere is the textbook **charge-only cable** signature.

So, two concrete things, and please paste **text** back this time:

**1. Answer directly: did you swap to a known-DATA USB-C cable?** (One you've actually transferred files with — not the one that came in the box.) This is the single most likely fix.

**2. Run the live watch and force download mode.** In the Ubuntu terminal:

- Watch for new lines. Then `Ctrl+C`.

**That was it — a charge-only cable.** With the data cable, the board enumerated perfectly:

```
COM3  →  USB Serial Device   VID_303A & PID_1001   (MI_00 = CDC serial)
        + "USB JTAG/serial debug unit" (MI_02)
```

`VID 303A / PID 1001` = **Espressif native USB-Serial/JTAG**. So the board's USB-C is the chip's built-in USB (exactly as its schematic said), and it's live on **COM3**. (The pile of "Intel XTU Component — Degraded" entries are unrelated tuning-utility junk; ignore them.)

**Important consequence for the console:** because this USB is the **native USB-Serial/JTAG** — *not* a UART0 bridge — the `nsh` image we built (console on UART0 / GPIO43-44) would flash fine but show **no console here**. To actually *see* the NSH prompt over this USB, we need the **`usbnsh`** config (console routed to the USB-Serial/JTAG). That's also exactly what your VelaPaw plan wants long-term (console on USB, freeing GPIO43 for the servo). So let's build that.

Since `nuttx.bin` and esptool already live in the VM, the cleanest flash is **from the VM** — no file copy, no Windows esptool. Let me do both in parallel:

## Step 1 — build `usbnsh` (VM terminal)
The spinlock patch and esptool are already in place, so this is just a reconfigure + rebuild:

```bash
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$HOME/openvela/prebuilts/gcc/linux-x86_64/xtensa-esp32s3-elf/bin:$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH
cd ~/openvela
./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:usbnsh -j4 2>&1 | tee ~/build-usbnsh.log
echo "=== BUILD EXIT ${PIPESTATUS[0]} ==="
ls -lh nuttx/nuttx.bin
```

## Step 2 — hand the board to the VM (do this while it builds)
In VMware's menu bar: **VM → Removable Devices →** find the Espressif entry (likely *"Espressif USB JTAG/serial debug unit"* or *"USB Composite Device"*) **→ Connect (Disconnect from Host).** That moves it off Windows COM3 and into Ubuntu. Then confirm it appears:

```bash
ls -l /dev/ttyACM* 2>/dev/null && sudo dmesg | tail -5
```

Paste back: the **`usbnsh` BUILD EXIT** + `nuttx.bin` size, and whether **`/dev/ttyACM0`** shows up in the VM after the passthrough. Once both are good, the next step is a one-line `esptool write_flash` and then we open the console to catch the NSH prompt. 🎯

**SPI Interface:**
- MOSI: GPIO17

- Backlight: GPIO13 (PWM)

- Audio codec (ES8311) address: 0x18

- BCLK: GPIO8
- WS (LRCK): GPIO6
- DOUT (Speaker): GPIO5
- DIN (Microphone): GPIO7
- MCLK: GPIO4

- PA Enable: GPIO9

- Battery ADC: GPIO10
- Boot Button: GPIO0
- Power Hold: GPIO40
- Headphone Detection: GPIO3

Got the authoritative pinout from the config that actually ran on your board. Here's what's confirmed:

| Signal | ESP32-S3 pin | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| LCD MOSI | **GPIO1** | |
| LCD MISO | GPIO2 | (unused for display writes) |
| LCD SCLK | **GPIO5** | |
| LCD DC | **GPIO3** | |
| LCD **CS** | **not a GPIO** (`NC`) | **tied low on-board** — LCD is sole device on this SPI |
| LCD **RST** | **not a GPIO** (`NC`) | **on the TCA9554 expander** (EXIO1) |
| LCD Backlight | **GPIO6** | active-high |
| I²C SDA / SCL | **GPIO8 / GPIO7** | shared bus, TCA9554 @ 0x20 |
| Panel | ST7796, **320×480** | run landscape (swap-xy), **BGR**, **color-inverted** |

The two tricky bits are confirmed: **CS is hardwired** (so the driver needs no CS toggling), and **RST hangs off the TCA9554** (so we must bring up the I²C expander and release reset before init). That's exactly the lckfb-szpi pattern. Let me read that template so I can author precise edits.

#include <nuttx/config.h>

#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <debug.h>
#include <assert.h>
#include <nuttx/arch.h>
#include <nuttx/board.h>
#include <nuttx/ioexpander/pca9557.h>
#include <nuttx/ioexpander/gpio.h>

#include "esp32s3_i2c.h"
#include "esp32s3-szpi.h"

/****************************************************************************
 * Pre-processor Definitions
 ****************************************************************************/

/* | PCA9557 | ESP32S3 |
 * |---------|---------|
 * | SCL     | IO2     |
 * | SDA     | IO1     |
 * | A0      | 3V3     |
 * | A1      | GND     |
 * | A2      | GND     |
 */

#define ESP32S3_PCA9557_I2C_PORT       (0)
#define ESP32S3_PCA9557_I2C_ADDR       (0x19)
#define ESP32S3_PCA9557_I2C_CLOCK      (100 * 1000)

/* | PCA9557 | Peripherals |
 * |---------|-------------|
 * | IO0     | LCD_CS      |
 * | IO1     | PA_EN       |
 * | IO2     | DVP_PWDW    |
 */

#define ESP32S3_PCA9557_LCD_CS         (0)
#define ESP32S3_PCA9557_PA_EN          (1)
#define ESP32S3_PCA9557_DVP_PWDN       (2)

/****************************************************************************
 * Private Data
 ****************************************************************************/

struct pca9557_config_s g_pca9557_config =
{
  ESP32S3_PCA9557_I2C_ADDR,
  ESP32S3_PCA9557_I2C_CLOCK,
  NULL,
};

/****************************************************************************
 * Public Functions
 ****************************************************************************/

int esp32s3_pca9557_initialize(void)
{
  FAR struct ioexpander_dev_s *ioe;
  FAR struct i2c_master_s *i2c;
  int ret;

  i2c = esp32s3_i2cbus_initialize(ESP32S3_PCA9557_I2C_PORT);
  if (!i2c)
    {
      i2cerr("Initialize I2C bus failed!\n");
      return -EINVAL;
    }

  ioe = pca9557_initialize(i2c, &g_pca9557_config);
  if (!ioe)
    {
      i2cerr("Initialize PCA9557 failed!\n");
      return -EINVAL;
    }

  ret = gpio_lower_half(ioe, ESP32S3_PCA9557_LCD_CS, GPIO_OUTPUT_PIN, 0);
  if (ret)
    {
      gpioerr("Create GPIO LCD_CS pin device failed!\n");
    }

  ret = gpio_lower_half(ioe, ESP32S3_PCA9557_PA_EN, GPIO_OUTPUT_PIN, 1);
  if (ret)
    {
      gpioerr("Create GPIO PA_EN pin device failed!\n");
    }

  ret = gpio_lower_half(ioe, ESP32S3_PCA9557_DVP_PWDN, GPIO_OUTPUT_PIN, 2);
  if (ret)
    {
      gpioerr("Create GPIO DVP_PWDW pin device failed!\n");
    }

  return 0;
}

Found it. `assert.c` only touches `LED_PANIC`/`LED_ASSERTION` under `#ifdef CONFIG_ARCH_LEDS`, and the esp32s3-devkit `board.h` **doesn't define those constants** — which is why *every* stock esp32s3-devkit defconfig carries an explicit `# CONFIG_ARCH_LEDS is not set`. My hand-written minimal defconfig omitted that line, so kconfig used the board's default (`y`) and pulled in the LED path. Simple fix: disable it.

## Fix — disable ARCH_LEDS, rebuild

```bash
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$HOME/openvela/prebuilts/gcc/linux-x86_64/xtensa-esp32s3-elf/bin:$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH

# esp32s3-devkit board.h has no LED_PANIC/LED_ASSERTION -> ARCH_LEDS must be OFF
echo '# CONFIG_ARCH_LEDS is not set' >> ~/openvela/nuttx/boards/xtensa/esp32s3/esp32s3-devkit/configs/waveshare_lcd/defconfig

cd ~/openvela
# re-apply spinlock patch (reconfigure re-clones the HAL again)
HAL=nuttx/arch/xtensa/src/esp32s3/esp-hal-3rdparty
grep -rlE 'define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+0[[:space:]]*$' "$HAL" 2>/dev/null \
  | xargs -r sed -i -E 's/(define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+)0[[:space:]]*$/\1SP_UNLOCKED/'

./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:waveshare_lcd -j4 2>&1 | tee ~/build-lcd.log
echo "=== BUILD EXIT ${PIPESTATUS[0]} ==="
ls -lh nuttx/nuttx.bin
```

The patch reverted again — but I see the exact ordering bug now. The sed ran *before* `build.sh`, and then `build.sh`'s configure step **re-cloned the HAL fresh** (the `Cloning Espressif HAL…` line appears *during* the build), wiping the patch I'd just applied. The patch has to go **after** the clone.

The fix is simply: patch now (the HAL is freshly cloned and unpatched on disk), then rebuild — this second `build.sh` won't reconfigure (config is unchanged), so it won't re-clone, and it'll compile with the patch intact. This is the same two-step that worked before.

```bash
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$HOME/openvela/prebuilts/gcc/linux-x86_64/xtensa-esp32s3-elf/bin:$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH
cd ~/openvela

# patch the freshly-cloned HAL (now, AFTER the clone)
HAL=nuttx/arch/xtensa/src/esp32s3/esp-hal-3rdparty
grep -rlE 'define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+0[[:space:]]*$' "$HAL" \
  | xargs -r sed -i -E 's/(define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+)0[[:space:]]*$/\1SP_UNLOCKED/'
echo "--- patched: ---"; grep -rnE 'LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED +SP_UNLOCKED' "$HAL"

# rebuild — config unchanged now, so NO re-clone
./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:waveshare_lcd -j4 2>&1 | tee ~/build-lcd.log
echo "=== BUILD EXIT ${PIPESTATUS[0]} ==="
ls -lh nuttx/nuttx.bin
```

The `--- patched: ---` line should show both files as `SP_UNLOCKED` before the build runs. Then it should compile past the HAL and (hopefully) all the way through — ARCH_LEDS is now off, so `assert.c` is fine too.

**Build is green (`BUILD EXIT 0`, `nuttx.bin` 204K)** — the spinlock two-step worked. But there's a telling warning:

```
esp32s3_bringup.c:521: warning: implicit declaration of function 'board_lcd_initialize'

Line 521 is the `#elif defined(CONFIG_LCD)` branch — which only compiles if **`CONFIG_VIDEO_FB` is OFF**. So kconfig **dropped `VIDEO_FB`** (it needs `CONFIG_DRIVERS_VIDEO`, which my defconfig didn't include). Consequences: no `/dev/fb0`, the `fb` app likely got dropped too, and `board_lcd_getdev()` (which actually runs the ST7789 init) never gets called — so the current binary would light the **backlight** but show no image.

Let me add the framebuffer stack deps and rebuild properly (with the build→patch→build dance baked in):

```bash

grep -q DRIVERS_VIDEO $D || printf 'CONFIG_DRIVERS_VIDEO=y\nCONFIG_VIDEO=y\n' >> $D

cd ~/openvela
# build #1: reconfigures + re-clones HAL (will fail on spinlock) — silence it
./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:waveshare_lcd -j4 >/tmp/b1.log 2>&1
# patch the freshly-cloned HAL
HAL=nuttx/arch/xtensa/src/esp32s3/esp-hal-3rdparty
grep -rlE 'define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+0[[:space:]]*$' "$HAL" \
  | xargs -r sed -i -E 's/(define[[:space:]]+LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED[[:space:]]+)0[[:space:]]*$/\1SP_UNLOCKED/'
# build #2: no reconfigure -> compiles with patch
./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:waveshare_lcd -j4 2>&1 | tee ~/build-lcd.log
echo "=== BUILD EXIT ${PIPESTATUS[0]} ==="

ls -lh nuttx/nuttx.bin
```

# Waveshare ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5 Board Analysis

## (1) TCA9554 Expander Usage

The TCA9554 I2C expander controls two pins:

```c
esp_io_expander_set_dir(io_expander, IO_EXPANDER_PIN_NUM_0 | IO_EXPANDER_PIN_NUM_1, 
                        IO_EXPANDER_OUTPUT);
esp_io_expander_set_level(io_expander, IO_EXPANDER_PIN_NUM_0 | 
                          IO_EXPANDER_PIN_NUM_1, 0);
vTaskDelay(pdMS_TO_TICKS(100));
esp_io_expander_set_level(io_expander, IO_EXPANDER_PIN_NUM_1, 1);
```

**Sequence:** Both pins 0 and 1 set low, then pin 1 set high (likely LCD power enable and reset control). The code provides no explicit mapping to LCD functions (reset/CS/backlight).

## (2) LCD SPI Chip-Select

The CS is **driven by ESP32 GPIO directly**, not the expander:

```c
io_config.cs_gpio_num = DISPLAY_CS_PIN;
```

## (3) ST7796 Panel Init

Uses **custom init command sequence**:

```c
esp_lcd_new_panel_st7789(panel_io, &panel_config, &panel);
```

with vendor config containing 17 initialization commands (0x11 sleep exit, 0x3A pixel format, 0xE0/0xE1 gamma curves, etc.).

## (4) Panel Settings

- `invert_color`: `DISPLAY_INVERT_COLOR` (macro value not shown)
- **RGB order:** `DISPLAY_RGB_ORDER`
- **Mirror X/Y:** `DISPLAY_MIRROR_X`, `DISPLAY_MIRROR_Y`
- **Swap XY:** `DISPLAY_SWAP_XY`
- **Offsets:** `DISPLAY_OFFSET_X`, `DISPLAY_OFFSET_Y`

All settings applied via `esp_lcd_panel_*` calls post-init.

## PMIC Class & I2C Address
The `Pmic` class extends `Axp2101` and is instantiated at I2C address `0x34`:

- `WriteReg(0x82, (3300 - 1500) / 100)` – Set DC1 to **3.3V**

The lckfb select callback confirms it: that board **actively drives CS per transaction** (via its expander) using the **software-CS path** (`SWCS`). Ours uses the hardware-CS path with `cs=-1`, and on the ESP32-S3 that path sets up CS timing for a chip-select that never asserts — which can leave the transaction ungated so **data never actually latches into the panel**, even though the clock "runs." That would perfectly explain invisible writes with no error. The working board sidesteps it entirely with `SWCS`.

Since `RDDID` is a dead signal (no MISO), the **screen itself** is now our only oracle. Let me switch to the proven software-CS transport and match lckfb's write-only MISO. This is a **config change** (defconfig), grounded in the shipping board that works:

```bash

D=~/openvela/nuttx/boards/xtensa/esp32s3/esp32s3-devkit/configs/waveshare_lcd/defconfig

# software CS transport (matches the working lckfb ST7789 board); panel is write-only
grep -q 'CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI_SWCS=y' "$D" || echo 'CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI_SWCS=y' >> "$D"
if grep -q 'CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MISOPIN' "$D"; then
  sed -i 's/^CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MISOPIN=.*/CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MISOPIN=-1/' "$D"
else
  echo 'CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MISOPIN=-1' >> "$D"
fi
echo "--- SPI lines now in defconfig ---"
grep -E 'SPI_SWCS|SPI2_MISOPIN|SPI2_MOSIPIN|SPI2_CLKPIN|SPI2_CSPIN' "$D"

cd ~/openvela

grep -E 'SPI_SWCS|SPI2_MISOPIN' nuttx/.config
cd ~/openvela/nuttx && python3 -m http.server 8000

In my SPI test, the CASET/RASET/RAMWR **commands** are 1-byte → *poll* path, but the 480-byte pixel **rows** are → *DMA* path. "All black" is exactly what you'd get if **poll works (window set) but DMA silently fails (no pixels written)** — the classic ESP32-S3 GDMA setup bug.

That's a concrete, testable hypothesis: **disable SPI DMA so everything uses the poll path.** If the red rectangle appears, we've got working hardware SPI (poll-mode) — plenty fast for the UI, and far quicker than bit-bang:

460 ms — **identical** to the 4-NOP version. That's actually the key finding: **the NOP delay was never the bottleneck** — it's the raw **GPIO register writes** (3 per bit ≈ 7.4M writes/frame at ~15 cycles each). Trimming NOPs can't help.

The real lever is **fewer writes per bit.** I can drop from 3 to 2 by writing the whole `GPIO_OUT_REG` with a shadow value (data+clock in one write, preserving the other pins), which should cut ~1/3 → ~300 ms. Let me do that:

```bash
export PATH=$HOME/bin:$HOME/openvela/prebuilts/gcc/linux-x86_64/xtensa-esp32s3-elf/bin:$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH

python3 - "$F" <<'PY'
import sys
f=sys.argv[1]; s=open(f).read()
s=s.replace('#define REG_W1TC 0x6000400CU      /* GPIO_OUT_W1TC_REG (pins 0-31) */',
            '#define REG_W1TC 0x6000400CU      /* GPIO_OUT_W1TC_REG (pins 0-31) */\n#define REG_OUT  0x60004004U      /* GPIO_OUT_REG (pins 0-31) */')
s=s.replace('static inline void dly(void){ __asm__ volatile("nop"); }\n','')
s=s.replace('static inline void ffbyte(uint8_t b)','static inline void ffbyte(uint8_t b, uint32_t base)')
old='''      if (b & 0x80) wreg(REG_W1TS, MOSI_M); else wreg(REG_W1TC, MOSI_M);
      b <<= 1;

      wreg(REG_W1TS, CLK_M);
      dly();
      wreg(REG_W1TC, CLK_M);'''
new='''      uint32_t o = base | ((b & 0x80) ? MOSI_M : 0);
      b <<= 1;
      wreg(REG_OUT, o);            /* data + CLK low */
      wreg(REG_OUT, o | CLK_M);    /* CLK high = sample */'''

s=s.replace(old,new)

text:
Done — clean production image flashed. **You now have a working display stack on real hardware.** 🎉

## What's built and on the board
- **`/dev/fb0` framebuffer** (480×320, RGB565) backed by a NuttX `lcd_dev` driver in the board file
- **ST7796** brought up over bit-bang: correct colors, correct per-region windowing, backlight via `setpower`
- **AXP2101 power + TCA9554 expander** init all in place
- Full-frame ~310 ms; **partial updates ~30 ms** (plenty for the feeder UI)
- Boots straight to a ready `/dev/fb0` (no self-test delay)

## The three bugs we killed (all in memory now)
1. **Byte order** — fb is little-endian, ST7796 wants high-byte-first → swap each pixel's bytes
2. **Windowing** — mixing `gpiowrite` + raw `GPIO_OUT_REG` left CLK high → corrupted the next `CASET` → unified everything onto one shadow-register routine that always ends CLK low
3. Earlier: the SPI peripheral dead-end → bit-bang (parked the peripheral for a logic-analyzer session)

## Next step (whenever you're ready)
Point **LVGL's fbdev driver at `/dev/fb0`** and build the first VelaPaw screen. In openVela that's typically enabling the LVGL fb port (`CONFIG_LV_USE_...` / the `lvgldemo` or an LVGL app opening `/dev/fb0`), then LVGL's flush callback lands in our `putarea` automatically. Small/dirty-rect redraws will be smooth; full-screen transitions ~⅓ sec.

This was a genuine hardware bring-up marathon — power, panel, a hidden SPI-peripheral fault, then the full framebuffer stack — and it's all working and documented. Want to tackle the LVGL wiring next, or pause here?

I found it in my notes — and this is important context: your emulator VelaPaw app is a **full application** (`app/velapaw/` → `packages/demos/contest2026_043_velapaw`), with `ui_lvgl.c` (Enroll/Recognize/My Pets/Trends tabs, camera preview, BCS, analytics), TFLM inference (identity + BCS models, ~2 MB), and camera HAL. It was built and runs in the **emulator (goldfish, 1280×800)**. That's a much bigger thing than a starter screen — and it lives in a **different tree** (`D:\openVela` contest repo) than the esp32s3 build we've been using (VM `~/openvela`).

**Honest scoping — porting the full app to this board is a real multi-part project:**

1. **Move the app** `app/velapaw/` into the esp32s3 tree and get it building for the ESP32-S3 target.
2. **UI redesign for 480×320.** The emulator UI is a **600 px-wide portrait column on a 1280×800** screen — that's *wider than our entire 480 px display*. The tabs/cards/chart all need re-layout for the small panel.
3. **Camera:** emulator used mock/webcam; hardware has the **OV5640** (a separate camera bring-up over the DVP interface).
4. **TFLM on the LX7:** your models run in the emulator (ARM); on-device LX7 latency is the #1 risk you flagged — needs measuring, maybe ESP-NN kernels.

Each of 2–4 is its own focused effort. Given how much we've already done this session (power → panel → SPI diagnosis → framebuffer → LVGL → touch → a working starter UI), I'd **checkpoint here** and tackle the port as a fresh, well-scoped push.

My suggested order for next time: **(a)** copy the app into the esp32s3 tree and stub out camera/TFLM so it builds, **(b)** re-lay-out `ui_lvgl.c` for 480×320 with mock data so the *real* screens show on the panel, then **(c)** wire the OV5640, then **(d)** TFLM + latency.

How do you want to proceed — **start the app port now** (beginning with getting it into the tree + UI re-layout), or **bank this milestone** and pick up the port next session? Either way, everything's saved in memory, and you have a genuinely working touchscreen device to build on.

**Our cadence is the limiting factor:** every change = build → download → manual BOOT/RESET flash → power-cycle → test through a flaky console. That's ~5–10 min *per iteration* even when nothing's wrong, and debugging is many iterations.

| Phase | What | Realistic time |

TWO bugs that cost hours: (1) **byte order** — NuttX fb is RGB565 little-endian, ST7796 wants high-byte-first → in putarea/putrun stream `p[i+1]` then `p[i]` (swap each pixel). (2) **CRITICAL windowing bug** — mixing esp32s3_gpiowrite (W1TS/W1TC, for commands) with raw GPIO_OUT_REG whole-writes (for pixels) left CLK HIGH after a fill, so the next CASET's first bit had no rising edge → window never changed → every fill went full-screen (uniform). FIX = **unify ALL bytes (command+data) onto ONE shadow-register routine** (`clock_byte` via GPIO_OUT_REG, D/C carried in the shadow `g_out`, and every byte routine ends CLK low with `wreg(REG_OUT,base)`). lcdfb calls putarea(rs,re,cs,ce, run=fbmem+starty*stride+startx*2, stride) — per-row `p=buffer+r*stride`, stream (ce-cs+1)*2 bytes. Needs CONFIG_FB_UPDATE=y (fb app flushes via FBIO_UPDATE→lcdfb→putarea; lcdfb also flushes once at init). Reminder: adding any defconfig sym re-clones esp-hal → re-apply the LOCK_INITIALIZER_UNLOCKED→SP_UNLOCKED sed, and `strings nuttx.bin | grep <marker>` to confirm the build actually relinked. **LVGL RUNS (2026-07-07): widgets demo renders on the panel via /dev/fb0.** Enable set on waveshare_lcd defconfig: `CONFIG_GRAPHICS_LVGL=y, LV_USE_NUTTX=y` (its NuttX port auto-opens /dev/fb0), `LV_USE_CLIB_MALLOC/SPRINTF/STRING=y, LV_USE_DEMO_WIDGETS=y, LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_20=y, EXAMPLES_LVGLDEMO=y`; resulting `LV_COLOR_DEPTH=16` matches our RGB565 (LVGL writes native little-endian → our putarea's byte-swap makes colors correct). **PSRAM is REQUIRED** (widgets demo OOMs on ~200KB internal SRAM after the 300KB fb): `CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPIRAM=y, ESP32S3_SPIRAM_MODE_OCT=y, ESP32S3_SPIRAM_SPEED_80M=y, MM_REGIONS=2` (adds the R8's 8MB as heap region 2). Also bumped EXAMPLES_LVGLDEMO_STACKSIZE=32768. Binary ~568KB (flash 0x0). Run: `lvgldemo widgets` (also benchmark/music/stress). NO TOUCH yet (FT6336 on I2C not wired — left LV_USE_NUTTX_TOUCHSCREEN off; demo is display-only). NOTE: the Windows .NET SerialPort console is UNRELIABLE for capturing command/crash output (shows stale NSH banners) — trust the SCREEN, and dmesg only sometimes. **TOUCH WORKS (2026-07-07): FT6336 interactive in LVGL.** FT6336 = FT5x06-compatible @ I2C0 0x38 (chip-id reg 0xA3=0x64). Enable: `CONFIG_INPUT_FT5X06=y, FT5X06_POLLMODE=y` (polls via workqueue — NO interrupt needed, avoids the expander TP_INT), `FT5X06_SINGLEPOINT=y, INPUT=y, INPUT_TOUCHSCREEN=y, SCHED_WORKQUEUE=y, SCHED_LPWORK=y, LV_USE_NUTTX_TOUCHSCREEN=y, EXAMPLES_LVGLDEMO_INPUT_DEVPATH="/dev/input0"`. Register in board_lcd_initialize: `ft5x06_config_s{.address=0x38,.frequency=400000,.wakeup=stub,.nreset=stub}` (pollmode needs only wakeup/nreset non-NULL) then `ft5x06_register(i2c,&cfg,0)` → /dev/input0. **TWO driver bugs I had to patch in drivers/input/ft5x06.c:** (1) it doesn't implement **TSIOC_GETMAXPOINTS** → lv_nuttx_touchscreen_create gets -ENOTTY and returns NULL → LVGL silently has no touch. Add an ioctl case returning `*(uint8_t*)arg = 1`. (2) **coord mapping** for our landscape display: the panel reports portrait, so in ft5x06_sample set `point.x = touch_Y; point.y = 320 - touch_X` (clamp 0..479 / 0..319). Derived from corner taps: TL(286,35) TR(286,443) BL(21,31) BR(30,440) Center(159,228). Touch is now interactive but the bit-bang display makes the heavy widgets demo sluggish (~2-3 fps); VelaPaw's lighter screens (small partial redraws ~30ms) will be fine. Next: build the VelaPaw screens.
47	
48	**310 ms is ~the bit-bang floor** (2 writes/bit is near-minimal); big further speedup needs the real SPI peripheral (parked, needs scope). Partial updates scale with area (~31 ms for 1/10 screen → snappy for the feeder UI). Or fix the real SPI peripheral (needs a logic analyzer — see above). TODO: wire the working bit-bang behind a minimal lcd_dev (putarea) so LVGL/fb can use it. NOTE: getdev returning NULL logs a harmless "Failed to initialize Frame Buffer Driver".
49	
50	## (superseded) LCD status (2026-07-06 earlier) — thought AXP2101 power fixed it (it did NOT; bit-bang above is the truth)
51	**THE FIX (after hours of white screen): the ST7796 logic rail is powered by the on-board AXP2101 PMIC (I2C 0x34), which our firmware never initialized → chip unpowered → register reads all 0xFF, blank/white panel.** Vendor power seq (from Xiaozhi board .cc; done BEFORE display init): AXP2101 enable **ALDO1=3.3V (reg0x92=(3300-500)/100), BLDO1=1.5V (0x96), BLDO2=2.8V (0x97), then reg0x90 |= 0x31** (enable ALDO1|BLDO1|BLDO2). Also DC1=3.3V (0x82) but avoid touching reg0x80 DCDC-enable (risks the ESP32 rail). Implemented as raw I2C writes to 0x34 in `board_lcd_initialize` (helpers axp_wr/axp_rd) on the same I2C0 bus (pins 7/8) — after i2cbus_init, before TCA9554/SPI. Once powered, the ST7796 lights up. **Remaining polish (all minor now):** filled GREEN(0x07E0) but panel showed BLUE → fix color order (BGR / byte-endian / `LCD_ST7789_INVCOLOR` / `_BGR` / `_DATA_ENDIAN_LITTLE`); remove the debug green-fill + RDDID reads from board_lcd_getdev; the `fb` app needs `CONFIG_FB_UPDATE` to flush its own draws; tune orientation (SWAP_XY/mirror) + offsets. Panel init: we send an ST7796 17-cmd vendor sequence over SPI in board code (st7796_init_and_fill) since NuttX has no ST7796 driver (ST7789 driver used only for the fb/putarea plumbing).
52	
53	## (superseded) earlier LCD dead-end — panel stayed WHITE; was the AXP2101 power (above)
54	Config `esp32s3-devkit:waveshare_lcd` (files: `configs/waveshare_lcd/defconfig` + `src/esp32s3_st7789.c`, DC set to GPIO3 in `esp32s3-devkit.h`). **Builds, flashes, boots.** **CONFIRMED WORKING via RAMLOG dmesg** (`[wslcd]` syslog): backlight GPIO6, **TCA9554 expander via `pca9557` driver @0x20 (`expander writes ret=0`** — drives IO_0 low + IO_1 reset pulse, matching Xiaozhi's both-pins sequence), SPI2 init, `st7789_lcdinitialize -> OK`, `/dev/fb0` (480×320 RGB565), `fb` example runs. **NOT working:** panel is backlit + powered but shows **clean white — no image.**
55	**Diagnosis (definitive):** NuttX has **no ST7796 driver**; the ST7789 driver's generic init (it DOES send SLPOUT/DISPON) is **insufficient to turn on the ST7796's pixels**. `lcdfb_initialize` does a full black flush at startup, which would show BLACK if SPI reached an on panel — it's white → panel not displaying. **FIX NEEDED: send the ST7796 vendor init** (Xiaozhi `.cc` uses `esp_lcd_new_panel_st7789` + a 17-cmd vendor array: 0x11 SLPOUT, 0x3A COLMOD=0x55, 0xF0 cmd-set unlock, 0xC0-C5 power, 0xE0/E1 gamma, 0x29 DISPON). Approach options: send these raw over SPI in board code before/around st7789 init (careful st7789 SWRESET doesn't wipe), or write a minimal st7796 driver. Also add **`CONFIG_FB_UPDATE`** (the `fb` app's FBIO_UPDATE is `#ifdef CONFIG_FB_UPDATE`, else it never flushes app draws). Cheap extra check: lower `CONFIG_LCD_ST7789_FREQUENCY` 40M→10M (signal integrity). Xiaozhi panel: SWAP_XY, BGR, INVERT_COLOR, 480×320.
